---
title: "1. The Chemical Core"
---

Here is a small mystery almost every tea drinker has lived through.

You buy two boxes. Both say "tea." One pours pale and grassy. The other pours dark and malty. One leaves you gently alert. The other can feel stronger, more "coffee-adjacent." Same grocery aisle. Same word on the label. So what changed—the plant, the factory, or the way you steeped it?

::: {.callout-tip}
**New to tea labels?** Start with **[Tea basics](../../tea-basics.qmd)**—a short aisle-to-cup map (what *English Breakfast*, *matcha*, bag vs loose, and herbal "tea" usually mean)—then come back here for the chemistry.
:::

This chapter answers that question in order—in plain kitchen language. First we meet the **tea plant** behind almost all commercial tea (one species, two everyday leaf personalities). Then we watch what happens after picking—when makers either **stop** the leaf from browning (green tea) or **let** it brown in air (black tea). Then we watch hot water act like a selective extractor: some guests leave the leaf early; one needs more heat and time. Finally we meet three named guests who arrive on different clocks: **caffeine** (wake-up), **L-theanine** (calm focus), and **EGCG** (a major green-tea plant compound).

You do **not** need Latin variety names, enzyme labels, molecular formulas, or dense dose tables to follow the open story. Those details live in collapsed **More detail** boxes. Tap a footnote marker to jump to the source, then tap the caret to jump back. Hover often shows a popup too.

By the end you will know why "what's in my mug?" is not one number—and why that mug sets up everything that happens in Chapter 2, after you swallow.

::: {.callout-tip title="Everyday words for this journey"}
- **Tea plant** — the bush behind almost all commercial tea (lab name in the foldout).
- **Stop browning / let it brown** — the factory fork that makes green vs black from the same leaf.
- **Extraction** — hot (or cold) water pulling compounds out of the leaf into your mug.
- **Three guests** — wake-up (caffeine), calm-focus (L-theanine), and the standout green-tea plant compound (EGCG).
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="More detail: lab words you may meet in foldouts"}
- **Camellia sinensis** — the tea plant species.
- **China type / Assam type** — two main plant styles (smaller cool-hill vs larger warm-lowland on average).
- **Oxidation / PPO** — leaf enzymes + air darken the leaf; heat can lock those enzymes off.
- **Catechins / theaflavins / thearubigins** — simple green-tea compounds vs darker black-tea pigments.
- **EGCG** — short for epigallocatechin-3-gallate; the standout catechin in green tea.
:::

## A drinker's field guide (still fact-based)

Before you leave the chemical core, here is a short field guide—the kind of thing you can keep in your head on a weekday morning. Dense numbers live in the foldout below; the open list stays practical.

**If you want grassy and plant-compound-forward:** choose green (or lightly browned) tea, use water that is hot but not a rolling boil for greens, and give the slower guest time to dissolve without cooking the cup into bitterness.[^1]

**If you want malt and body:** choose black tea. You are choosing the "let it brown" factory path on purpose—the darker pigments are the mouthfeel makers.[^2]

**If you care about calm focus as well as wake-up:** remember that ordinary cups deliver **tens of milligrams** of L-theanine, not the **100–200 mg** capsules used in many lab trials.[^3][^4] A matcha or shaded green can climb higher; a quick black bag is usually lower on theanine and higher on the "familiar caffeine" side (see [Cup reference](../../cup-reference.qmd)).

**If someone says cold brew is caffeine-free:** smile, then remember the clock. Cold only slows the exit of caffeine from the leaf.[^5] Time is the real variable.

**If someone says Assam always doubles China caffeine:** remember the cultivar survey and the pack's counter-examples. Averages lean Assam-higher; gardens and plucking standards write the fine print.[^6]

**If you want the tasting-lab strength:** lab sensory cups are often stronger than many home mugs.[^7] The [Cup reference](../../cup-reference.qmd) sticks to the everyday baseline so lab and kitchen do not get confused.

None of that is medical advice. It is plant chemistry meeting a kettle—with sources you can check.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: numbers behind the field guide"}
- Green-tea extraction work maps how temperature and time change catechin and caffeine recovery; pushing heat and time too far can destroy the compounds you hoped to pull.[^1]
- Black-tea pigments (theaflavins → thearubigins) form when makers let enzymes meet air.[^2]
- Keenan and colleagues measured real-cup L-theanine; Owen and colleagues used known capsule milligrams in cognition trials.[^3][^4]
- Infusion kinetics: cold slows caffeine exit; it does not delete it.[^5]
- Takeda's cultivar survey: Assam-group mean caffeine higher on average than China-group—still not a guarantee for any one tin.[^6]
- ISO 3103 (sensory preparation) uses about **2 g leaf per 100 mL** boiling water—roughly **5 g per 250 mL**—stronger than many home cups that use about **2 g per 250 mL**.[^7]
:::

## Looking ahead

You now know how a plant becomes a cup, and which three characters usually steal the scene. The next chapter picks up exactly where this one leaves off: **after you swallow**. Why does tea so often feel different from coffee? What do brain waves, stress hormones, and body signals actually show?

Open [Chapter 2: Body, Brain & Mood](../module-02/index.qmd) when you are ready—the compounds have already started their trip.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Click for more detail: a one-page chemical checklist"}
- Same species, two main plant styles: China-type vs Assam-type averages differ, gardens decide the fine print.[^8][^6]
- Green vs black is mostly a **processing fork** (kill browning enzymes with heat vs let oxidation run), not a different plant in ordinary commercial tea.[^9][^2][^10]
- Brewing is extraction: caffeine and L-theanine come out easily; EGCG wants more heat/time and can degrade if you overcook it.[^5][^3][^1]
- Three guests, three clocks: caffeine hours, L-theanine tens of minutes, EGCG in between—so "I just sipped" ≠ peak effect.[^11][^12][^13]
- Lab capsules (e.g. 100–200 mg L-theanine) are not grocery-bag cups; check the [Cup reference](../../cup-reference.qmd).[^3][^4]
:::
